item.title: DISCOVERING FIJI I Rev Thomas Baker (Part 1)
item.description: LONG before Reverend Thomas Baker’s name became forever linked with one of Fiji’s most tragic chapters, it was tied to something far quieter, a deep conviction that his life’s work lay among the people of the islands. His own words, written years before his death reveal not fear but anticipation, a man convinced he had found his purpose.
item.content:encoded:
LONG before Reverend Thomas Baker’s name became forever linked with one of Fiji’s most tragic chapters, it was tied to something far quieter, a deep conviction that his life’s work lay among the people of the islands.

His own words, written years before his death reveal not fear but anticipation, a man convinced he had found his purpose.

“When I knew I was to go to Fiji I felt my spirit was glad,” he wrote in his diary on February 18, 1859.

“To this place I felt my spirit irresistibly drawn, and now I have my heart’s desire.”

Those diary entries, together with accounts preserved in The Missionary Worthies by Reverend William Moister, correspondence published in Missionary Enterprise and Home Service – An Autobiography by John S. Austin, and records from FamilySearch, paint the portrait of a missionary whose brief ministry was marked by unwavering faithfulness.

The Missionary Worthies by Reverend William Moister, kept at the Camden Theological Library archives highlight that Thomas Baker was born at Playden, Sussex in England, on February 6, 1832, to Jeremiah Baker and Harriett Elizabeth Vinten.

When he was eight years old, the family migrated to Australia where his life would take a direction he could scarcely have imagined.

Drawn by his love of singing, Baker began attending a Wesleyan church in Sydney.

There, according to Reverend Moister, he came “under the Ministry of the Word,” became convinced of sin and “soon experienced acceptance with God.”

His faith quickly became evident through his service.

After joining the Wesleyan Society, his “consistent piety and ardent zeal” led to his appointment as a class leader and local preacher.

In 1859 he married Harriett Moon in Chippendale, New South Wales. That same year he was accepted as a probationer by the Australian Wesleyan Conference and appointed as a missionary to Fiji.

The appointment was exactly what he had hoped for.

“And now I have great work to perform,” Reverend Baker wrote in his journal.

“I know God is my helper and in the strength of Grace I go far hence to the Gentiles.”

He believed the Gospel could reach even the darkest places.

“Truly the dark places of the earth are full of habitants of cruelty. But their darkness can be expelled by the light of the Gospel.”

Baker travelled to Fiji with Reverend Joseph Waterhouse and other missionaries, arriving on April 25, 1859, after a 16-day voyage aboard the John Wesley.

His first impressions of the islands reflected both admiration and the challenges ahead.

“My sickness for the first three days hindered me from enjoying the passage. My wife was very sick also,” he wrote.

“The John Wesley is one of the best cradles I ever was in.”

“I see here a very large field open to my view for missionary labour. The work appears to be very rough, plenty travelling by water.”

Despite the unfamiliar surroundings, Baker immersed himself in learning the Fijian language.

Reverend Moister records that before the end of Baker’s first year he was already preaching the Gospel in Fijian.

For more than eight years he served in the Bau, Cakaudrove, Bua and Rewa Circuits, gaining experience while frequently travelling through difficult terrain and by sea.

He often expressed a desire to work where the need was greatest and was delighted when appointed to Rewa.

There he regularly visited villages beyond established Christian communities, seeking to share his faith among those who had yet to embrace Christianity.

Letters Baker sent to his friend, Methodist Minister John S. Austin, offer a rare glimpse into daily missionary life in Fiji during the 1860s.

Writing on March 30, 1866, after moving from Bua into the interior of Viti Levu, Baker described living at what he considered the frontier between Christian and non-Christian communities.

“We have removed from Bua to the interior of large Fiji, the stronghold of Heathenism and a very large and important circuit,” he wrote.

item.title: CLIMATE SCIENCE I When highlands to the coasts shivered
item.description: THE July 2026 cold spell serves as a stark reminder that Fiji’s climate is governed by massive, natural synoptic systems rather than singular climate anomalies. As WMO accredited Class 1 Professional Meteorologist, it is essential for me to frame this event through the lens of atmospheric physics: a powerful, quasi-stationary high-pressure system—which registered a provisional record-breaking mean
item.content:encoded:
THE July 2026 cold spell serves as a stark reminder that Fiji’s climate is governed by massive, natural synoptic systems rather than singular climate anomalies.

As WMO accredited Class 1 Professional Meteorologist, it is essential for me to frame this event through the lens of atmospheric physics: a powerful, quasi-stationary high-pressure system—which registered a provisional record-breaking mean sea level pressure of 1044.5 hPa near Ouse, Tasmania, on July 6, 2026—acted as a giant atmospheric pump.

This high-pressure system was intensified by a deep low-pressure system lingering over the Tasman Sea, a process known as anticyclonic intensification, where diverging air from the upper levels of the low fed into the high-pressure system, forcing air to subside and intensify at the surface.

This synoptic setup established a persistent meridional flow, effectively funnelling a deep reservoir of polar-origin air masses directly into the tropical latitudes, including Fiji.

To understand why this cold spell was so pervasive, one must look at the “weather engine” driving the entire region. The blocking high-pressure system did not merely drift across the map; it stalled. In meteorology, we refer to this as a “blocking high”—a strong system that forms further south than usual and remains nearly stationary.

This effectively “blocked” the typical west-to-east progression of weather systems across the Southern Hemisphere, locking a specific atmospheric state in place for over a week.

The intensification was fuelled by a deep low-pressure system sitting over the Tasman Sea. When a high and a low pair in this specific configuration, they create a “blocking pair,” which serves to mutually reinforce the strength of both systems. As air converged in the upper atmosphere, it subsided rapidly, creating a process of divergence at the surface that intensified the high to historic levels.

This generated a steep pressure gradient, transforming the region into a potent meridional conduit that drew a massive, coherent air mass from high latitudes and funnelled it directly into the tropical South Pacific.

Unlike transient weather fluctuations that pass in a matter of hours, this cold air mass stagnated over the region, creating a sustained “cool-down” effect that refused to dissipate, replacing the typical tropical maritime air with a polar-origin mass.

The intensity of this event was felt cohesively across the Fiji Group, revealing a national drop in temperatures that defied the typical tropical baseline. In the Western Division, covering Nadi, Lautoka, and Ba, the cold air mass pushed minimums significantly lower than typical July averages.

Even in these traditionally warmer regions, where residents are accustomed to the reliable warmth of the leeward side, the persistence of the high-pressure system ensured that nights remained unusually chilly, with breezy conditions adding to the cooling effect. Moving to the Eastern Division, including Lauthala Bay, Nausori, and Navua, the impact was even more pronounced.

The eastern coast, often directly subject to the persistent southeasterly trade winds, bore the full brunt of this advection. Navua, in particular, shattered records on July 5, 2026, dropping to 13.8°C—the lowest reading since observations began there in 2010.

This impact was mirrored in the Maritime Groups, where stations at Matei, Vanuabalavu, and Kadavu confirmed the widespread nature of the event. Matei Airfield recorded 14.5°C on July 10, the lowest since 1956, while Vanuabalavu hit 14.6°C on July 3, the lowest since 1985. These isolated stations provided the clearest evidence that this was a total regional air-mass replacement rather than a localized fluctuation.

While Nadarivatu remained the coldest point, bottoming out at 9.7°C, the Fiji Meteorological Service noted this was not a new record, but rather a validation of its status as the nation’s traditional highland “cold trap.” It should be noted that these are only sparse point observations, and many locations across Fiji who do not have observations, multiple locations would have hit extreme lows.

Nadarivatu’s role as Fiji’s “cold trap” is rooted in its unique topography, perched at an elevation of over 800 meters. Historically, this geography has allowed for temperate-zone agriculture, including potatoes and experimental apple orchards, which thrive in these cooler microclimates that remain impossible to cultivate on the coast.

The colonial-era use of Nadarivatu as a sanatorium further underscores how distinct this highland climate is from the coastal tropical norm, serving as a retreat for those seeking relief from the humidity. During this July event, the 9.7°C reading was not a statistical anomaly but a validation of its high-altitude role as the country’s natural thermometer.

For the local farmers, this cold spell was an intensification of the “cool and dry season” mechanism that defines their agricultural cycles. It highlights how elevation and topography dictate localized outcomes even when a singular air mass blankets the entire country.

The “record-breaking” nature of this event was magnified by the clear, dry conditions that accompanied the high-pressure system. With the sky devoid of cloud cover, Fiji experienced intense nocturnal radiative cooling, where heat from the surface escaped rapidly into the upper atmosphere.

In a three-dimensional sense, the atmosphere was effectively “layered,” with the dense, cold air mass trapped near the surface and unable to dissipate due to the lack of turbulent vertical mixing. This stability, combined with the daily replenishment of cold air from the Southern Ocean, meant that the “chill” was an enduring state for the entire archipelago rather than a passing front.

Because the air was dry, it lacked the moisture content to form clouds that might otherwise trap outgoing longwave radiation. Consequently, the ground cooled rapidly during the night, leading to the remarkably low minimums that residents across Fiji felt, regardless of whether they were in a coastal or inland valley.

This synoptic configuration extended its reach far beyond the Fiji Group. While Fiji basked in cool, dry stability, the deep low-pressure system driving the high brought severe weather to our neighbours.

In New Zealand, the system developed out of the Southern Ocean as a large, slow-moving low that drew cold air north, creating widespread convection and intense rainfall that overwhelmed infrastructure in places like Wellington.

This was not a tropical storm, but rather a cold-core low that produced localized downpours as it moved over the unusually warm Tasman Sea. Meanwhile, in southeastern Australia, the core of the high-pressure system caused temperatures to plunge, with areas like Coldstream dropping to -2.7°C and parts of Tasmania hitting -8.1°C, accompanied by dense fog and widespread frost.

This regional variety is the very definition of natural synoptic variability. It serves as a reminder that our weather is the product of complex interactions between air masses, pressure systems, and topography.

This event is a testament to the fascinating complexity of our regional climate system. It is a reminder that in the South Pacific, the movement of high-pressure engines can redefine the baseline of our daily weather, testing our tropical resilience and highlighting the raw, shifting physics that govern the weather we experience every day.

There is no cause for alarm; we have simply witnessed the atmospheric gears of the South Pacific shifting into a rare, high-intensity configuration, providing a brief but memorable respite from our typical tropical warmth, and high humidities leading to discomfort.

It is a classic demonstration of how large-scale, stationary high-pressure systems behave when they lock into place, reordering the climate of the entire region. We have observed the full force of a historically record breaking 1044.5 hPa high pressure, and in doing so, we have seen the natural variability of our planet at work—a humbling display of the meteorology that shapes our lives.

Dr SUSHIL K SHARMA (BA MA MEng (RMIT) PhD (Melbourne)) is a former World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) Accredited Class 1 Professional Meteorologist; Former British Aerospace, The Royal Saudi Air Force and Bahrain Air Navigation Directorate Aviation Meteorologist; Former Associate Professor of Meteorology, Fiji National University, and former Operational Meteorologist and Manager, Climate Research and Services Division, Fiji Meteorological Services. The views expressed are his and not necessarily shared by this newspaper.

item.title: WOMEN I Charting her own course
item.description: JANET Reddy still remembers one of the people who shaped the way she sees the world. Growing up, the late Justice Jai Ram Reddy was more than a distinguished statesman, jurist and constitutional architect.
item.content:encoded:
JANET Reddy still remembers one of the people who shaped the way she sees the world.

Growing up, the late Justice Jai Ram Reddy was more than a distinguished statesman, jurist and constitutional architect.

Her granddaughter, embodied the values of service, unity and thoughtful leadership.

Among the many lessons he left behind were his passion for genuine national unity and finding common ground, ideals that remain etched in Janet’s mind.

Years later, those values continue to guide the young environmental scientist as she prepares to begin a fully funded PhD in Marine Science and Conservation at Duke University in the United States, following her graduation from Cornell University, where she became the first Fijian known to complete an undergraduate degree at the Ivy League institution.

Although the pursuit for knowledge has taken her from a small farm outside Lautoka to some of the world’s leading universities, Janet said her purpose has never changed.

It is about giving back to Fiji by protecting the oceans that have shaped both the country’s identity and its future.

Janet completed her primary education at Drasa Avenue Primary School before attending Natabua High School, where she excelled in the sciences.

Leaving Fiji after Year 12 to study in the United States was both exciting and daunting.

She enrolled in Cornell University’s Environment and Sustainability programme without knowing exactly where her journey would lead.

“I wasn’t completely sure what I wanted to specialise in,” she said.

Rather than choosing a single pathway, she designed her own interdisciplinary concentration in Marine Conservation and Management.

“I’ve always been interested in bringing together science, policy and community perspectives.

“I wanted to combine my science background with studies in policy and decision-making because it’s one thing to produce scientific knowledge, but it’s equally important that decision-makers understand that science and that scientists understand the realities of policy.”

She said researchers and policymakers often speak different technical languages.

“Good decisions require everyone to work from the same understanding.”

While science has become her profession, public service has long been part of her family’s story.

She speaks warmly of her grandfather, Justice Jai Ram Reddy, whose speeches and commitment to national reconciliation continue to influence her thinking.

“Whenever I think about Fiji’s future, I often come back to that message,” she said.

“If I had to reduce Justice Jai Ram Reddy’s message to one word, it would be unity.”

For Janet, unity is not about ignoring differences but recognising that diversity strengthens a nation.

“We all have different histories, cultures and life experiences, but the important question is how those individual experiences contribute to a shared future.

“At the end of the day, we’re all Fijians.”

That philosophy was reinforced while representing Fiji and other Small Island Developing States as a United Nations Scotland Earth Ambassador.

Working alongside young leaders from around the world, she realised that diversity was not something that divided people but strengthened collective efforts towards a sustainable future.

Cornell challenged Janet academically and personally.

When she graduated earlier this year, she discovered she was believed to be the first Fiji-born student to graduate from the university.

“It filled me with immense pride, not simply as a personal achievement, but because of what it represented for Fiji and the Pacific.”

Initially searching for fellow Fijians and Pacific Islanders, she eventually realised that belonging extended beyond geography.

“My upbringing in Fiji gave me my foundation, while my experiences overseas broadened my perspective.

item.title: ACCOMPLISHMENT I Fiji in RUCI’s musical journey
item.description: LONG before she stood behind Australian music star Guy Sebastian as a backing vocalist, before recording her own songs and dreaming of releasing an album, Atelaite Ruci Tuiwai was a little girl standing beside her father in church. item.content:encoded:
LONG before she stood behind Australian music star Guy Sebastian as a backing vocalist, before recording her own songs and dreaming of releasing an album, Atelaite Ruci Tuiwai was a little girl standing beside her father in church.

Known in the music industry simply as RUCI, the Fiji-born singer’s musical journey began not under bright stage lights, but within the walls of the Methodist Church of Fiji, where her faith and music became inseparable.

“I started singing when I was three years old,” she said.

“My very first stage was at the Methodist Church of Fiji conference, where I sang with the choir led by my late father.”

Those early performances would lay the foundation for a career that has since taken her onto some of Australia’s biggest stages.

Yet despite the opportunities that have come her way, RUCI remains deeply connected to the values that shaped her childhood.

“I am from Lomaji, Kabara, in Lau, and share maternal links to Nadrala, Conua, Baravi in Nadroga,” she said.

“I have been living in Australia for the past 12 years, but Fiji will always be home.”

Her sense of identity extends far beyond geography.

“My identity is deeply rooted in my family, my faith and my vanua. Being iTaukei is more than just knowing where you come from; it is reflected in the values we carry through respect, humility, service and the responsibility of representing those who came before us.”

Much of RUCI’s childhood was spent along Fiji’s Coral Coast, where her late father served as a vakatawa (lay pastor) with the Methodist Church of Fiji for 16 years.

Those years were filled with church services, choir practices and family gatherings where music was part of everyday life.

“My father wasn’t just my dad, he was my mentor, my first music teacher and my biggest supporter,” she said.

“Music was part of our everyday life, and through him I learned that singing was never just about performing; it was about serving God and serving people.”

As she grew older, she found inspiration in the works of celebrated Fijian musicians, including Etuate Kautoga, better known as Eddie, whose choir compositions left a lasting impression.

She also admired legendary groups such as Black Rose, Waikoula kei Tavua and the traditional sigidrigi singing bands that remain central to many Fijian celebrations.

“What I love about Fijian music is the storytelling,” she said.

“The songs carry stories of families, villages, ancestry, relationships and traditions passed down through generations.”

That tradition of storytelling continues to influence the kind of artist she hopes to become.

Like many young people, RUCI considered different paths as she grew older.

For a time, she questioned whether music would become more than something she simply loved.

“People often say, ‘Your talent is your bread,’ and for a long time I wondered what that really meant,” she said.

“As I grew older, I realised that no matter what I studied or what career path I considered, music always found its way back to me.”

She credits fellow members of the Sydney-based Fijian band Oz Fijian Vibez for encouraging her to embrace her gift.

“The team constantly encouraged me to value the gift God had given me not only because I could sing, but because of the impact music can have on people’s lives.”

That encouragement strengthened her resolve to continue serving through music, whether as a worship leader, choir member or recording artist.

Today, her growing list of musical achievements includes her debut gospel single Me’u muri ga, which she co-composed and recorded with Lesaa.

She has also featured with VLY on the remake of the classic Fijian song O Nadroga okwe kodaki o Amerika and collaborated with the Domo ni Cakau group on Sevataki dina sara, a remake of the Black Rose classic.

“Each opportunity has taught me something different and continues to shape me as a musician and as a person,” she said.

One of the defining moments of RUCI’s career came without warning.

item.title: REFLECTION I Inspired by the sacred chime
item.description: THIS poem is inspired by the chime of a rooster in the distance outside my bedroom window each morn. Later, a family member who dwells in the countryside abroad, disclosed the fondness of her children of a rooster in their collection of farm pet animals and thus, I composed the poem in honour of their rooster pet, by the name of Kookie.
item.content:encoded:
THIS poem is inspired by the chime of a rooster in the distance outside my bedroom window each morn.

Later, a family member who dwells in the countryside abroad, disclosed the fondness of her children of a rooster in their collection of farm pet animals and thus, I composed the poem in honour of their rooster pet, by the name of Kookie.

People refer to the morn chime of a rooster as a ‘crow sound,’ which is vocalised by a high- decibel, prolonged sound that can be heard clearly over the distance of the dawn.

My reference and preference of their ‘crow sound’ as a chime is an acknowledgement of the sacred and supreme duty of such a sentient being as an alarm clock of nature.

Although roosters do not only and always awaken their flock at sunrise, their internal circadian clock is a natural chime clock at dawn that throughout time, has awakened people to a new day.

Sometimes, it is a pet animal who reminds their owner that breakfast is to be served with the sunrise!

Even a sundial crafted in simplicity through history is a clock as harmonious as nature.

The morn chimes that exist in equilibrium to the rhythmic resonance of the serene sounds of nature are parallel to the energy fields (aura, chakras and similar frequency fields) of the human mind and body, which is by creation itself, parallel to the frequency of earth.

Blessed be the land where the alarm clocks of nature are still revered — from the call of a rooster; the beat of a wooden drum (lali); a choir of birds singing at the sight of dawn to bells ringing from a church steeple or a monastery in the mountain.

The human energy fields are influenced by various states of (well) being — mental, emotional and physical states and their mutual alignment influences sleep patterns, states of mood and brainwave frequencies, which promote the vigour and vitality of positive health.

The placid tones of the chimes of nature — even a high- frequency chime of a rooster — serves to refresh and rejuvenate the mind and body in sleep for a new day because of their rhythmic resonance.

At each sunrise, my eyes awaken to the chime of a rooster in the distance, proceeded by the morn melodies of birds in the vicinity of my garden.

I am awake to offer my salutations to the sunrise and seek the blessings of the birds flying around me.

Nonetheless, it is the chime of the rooster that truly awakens my appreciation to the wonders of the natural world.

The soulful voice of a solitaire rooster in the distance to remind me to arise from slumber, is a most magical and mystical chime to activate my mind and align my mindfulness to my environment.

I can only imagine the beauty and blessing of a rooster chime in the vicinity of a farmhouse, where a family awakens together, prays together, attends to their chores together and stays together.

Likewise, a rooster whose chime can be heard at nightfall is often a signal of a period of personal and spiritual transformation.

The antics and anecdotes of Kookie the rooster on his farmland, was the inspiration for the other portion of the poem.

As relayed by the family, Kookie will be perched upon the farmyard gate — prefect of his property — to oversee the other farm animals or parade the length of the porch as proud as a peacock to monitor the morn and ensure that there is no friction amongst the flock and family in his care.

Such an enchanting childhood experience for the children of the family.

The precious and priceless moments and memories they will forever cherish.

The discipline, dedication to duty and awareness of the divinity of nature they will forever appreciate.

The skills they acquire upon their farmland through the seasons will be their travel companion as they sail through the journey of life.

Indeed, all the sentient animals on their farmland are nature’s teachers and the lessons they learn are sacred and supreme, as the education system of nature always is.

item.title: Grand Launch of TISA Insurance (Fiji) Ltd | Creating opportunity through inclusion
item.description: EVERY community deserves the opportunity to thrive. That belief has inspired TISA Insurance to support programmes that restore dignity and open doors for vulnerable members of society. Through partnerships with organisations such as Corona Fiji and Being Helping Hands Fiji, TISA supports dignity pack programs that provide essential hygiene products to young women and schoolgirls in rural communiti
item.content:encoded:
EVERY community deserves the opportunity to thrive. That belief has inspired TISA Insurance to support programmes that restore dignity and open doors for vulnerable members of society.

Through partnerships with organisations such as Corona Fiji and Being Helping Hands Fiji, TISA supports dignity pack programs that provide essential hygiene products to young women and schoolgirls in rural communities.

The items themselves are simple; their impact is profound. They help women protect their wellbeing and reinforce the importance of dignity and inclusion.

The company has also continued its partnership with Homes of Hope and Loloma Homes, supporting women and young girls who have experienced abuse and hardship.

By providing workplace exposure and practical learning opportunities, TISA is helping participants build confidence, develop valuable skills and prepare for independent futures.

These initiatives reflect a simple but powerful philosophy: empowering one individual can transform an entire family and, ultimately, a community.

Education remains one of the most powerful tools for lasting change, and TISA Insurance continues to support initiatives that improve access to learning, particularly for students in underserved communities.

Its partnership with the Foundation for the Education of Needy Children (FENC) has helped provide laptops and essential classroom furniture, giving students greater access to educational resources and digital learning.

Support for Rokotuivatu District School has helped establish a new computer laboratory, ensuring students in remote communities have opportunities comparable to those in urban centres.

These investments are about far more than computers and equipment.

They are investments in knowledge, confidence and the aspirations of young Fijians who will shape the country’s future.

item.title: Grand Launch of TISA Insurance (Fiji) Ltd | Expanding financial protection through innovation
item.description: INNOVATION sits at the heart of how TISA Insurance serves its customers. The Bancassurance Initiative of the Year, Fiji award recognises the company’s work with a leading financial services partner to make insurance a seamless part of everyday financial decisions.
item.content:encoded:
INNOVATION sits at the heart of how TISA Insurance serves its customers.

The Bancassurance Initiative of the Year, Fiji award recognises the company’s work with a leading financial services partner to make insurance a seamless part of everyday financial decisions.

The initiative simplifies the customer experience, supports responsible lending and brings financial protection within reach of everyday Fijians.

Strengthening Healthcare Access in Papua New Guinea.

The Strategic Partnership Initiative of the Year – Papua New Guinea award recognises an initiative that has transformed the way policyholders access essential healthcare services.

The initiative improves access to care at the moment it is needed most – a clear example of how the right partnership can improve customer outcomes while strengthening financial protection for communities across Papua New Guinea.

Driving Sustainable Growth Across Papua New Guinea Recognition as Domestic General Insurer of the Year – Papua New Guinea reflects sustained performance in one of the Pacific’s most diverse markets.

TISA Insurance has continued to expand insurance access while maintaining disciplined underwriting and prudent risk management and is investing in its capabilities to make insurance simpler and more accessible for thousands of members across the country.

These results are made possible by a culture built on collaboration, accountability and a shared commitment to excellence.

While these awards recognise business performance, they also acknowledge the company’s responsibilities to the communities it serves.

Across the Pacific, TISA Insurance continues to invest in initiatives that strengthen financial inclusion, support grassroots sport, empower women, encourage small business development and contribute to healthier, more resilient communities – because its impact should extend beyond the policies it underwrites.

These four awards belong to everyone who has been part of the TISA Insurance journey: its employees, customers, brokers, agents, partners, community organisations and stakeholders across the Pacific.

Their trust, partnership and support continue to inspire the company to keep improving, innovating and delivering on its promise.

As TISA Insurance begins this new chapter, the company remains focused on building a stronger, more resilient Pacific by providing trusted insurance solutions that create lasting value for customers and communities across Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Tonga, Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands.

TISA Insurance looks to the future with confidence, purpose and an unwavering commitment to protecting what matters most.

item.title: Grand Launch of TISA Insurance (Fiji) Ltd | A new chapter recognised across the Pacific
item.description: As TISA Insurance begins an exciting new chapter across the Pacific, the Group is proud to announce it has been honoured with four awards at the Insurance Asia Awards 2026 recognition of its commitment to protecting communities, driving innovation and delivering sustainable growth. These awards reflect the trust customers place in TISA Insurance, the dedication of its people, and the strength of t
item.content:encoded:
As TISA Insurance begins an exciting new chapter across the Pacific, the Group is proud to announce it has been honoured with four awards at the Insurance Asia Awards 2026 recognition of its commitment to protecting communities, driving innovation and delivering sustainable growth.

These awards reflect the trust customers place in TISA Insurance, the dedication of its people, and the strength of the partnerships that continue to shape its success across the region.

Across Fiji and Papua New Guinea, TISA Insurance Group was recognised in four categories:

International General Insurer of the Year;

Fiji, Bancassurance Initiative of the Year;

Fiji, Domestic General Insurer of the Year;

Papua New Guinea, Strategic Partnership Initiative of the Year – Papua New Guinea.

Together, these achievements reinforce TISA Insurance’s vision of building one of the Pacific’s leading insurance groups – one that strengthens financial resilience and expands access to protection for individuals, families, businesses and communities.

The International General Insurer of the Year – Fiji award reflects the company’s focus on disciplined growth, strong governance and long-term value for its customers.

TISA Insurance has continued to strengthen and diversify its business, broadening the range of solutions it offers and the ways customers can access them – ensuring more Fijians have access to quality insurance when and where they need it.

That progress rests on responsible underwriting, prudent pricing and effective claims management.

Above all, it rests on the company’s people, whose professionalism, technical expertise and customer-first approach turn strategy into meaningful outcomes every day.
